title: Photosynthesis
unit: AS (inferred from topic order; unit number not stated in source)

questions.question: Which row of the table shows the colour of each of the three seaweeds?
questions.answer: A: U. fasciata green, S. linifolium brown, C. officinalis red.
steps: U. fasciata has by far the most chlorophyll a and b, so chlorophyll hides other pigments and it is green.
C. officinalis has almost no chlorophyll b and relatively more carotenoids, which fits a red seaweed.
S. linifolium has less chlorophyll but its carotenoids give it a brown colour.
Row A is the only row with green, brown and red in this order.

questions.question: Explain the role of chloroplast pigments in the light-dependent reactions of photosynthesis.
questions.answer: Pigments absorb light energy to excite electrons, which pass along the electron transport chain to make ATP and reduced NADP.
steps: Chloroplast pigments absorb light energy at specific wavelengths.
This energy excites electrons to a higher energy level.
The electrons pass along an electron transport chain, releasing energy.
This energy makes ATP by chemiosmosis and reduces NADP.

questions.question: Describe how GALP, produced in chloroplasts, is converted into protein.
questions.answer: GALP is converted to intermediates such as pyruvate; nitrogen from nitrate is added to form amino acids, which are joined by peptide bonds at ribosomes.
steps: GALP is made in the light-independent reactions in the stroma.
GALP is converted into intermediates such as pyruvate, which provide the carbon skeletons.
Nitrate ions from the soil are reduced to supply nitrogen, and the nitrogen is added to form amino acids.
Amino acids are joined by condensation to form peptide bonds at ribosomes, guided by mRNA.

questions.question: Comment on the statement that these seaweeds are a healthy, environmentally friendly and economic food source, using the table and your own knowledge.
questions.answer: Partly supported: the table shows useful protein, carbohydrate and antioxidants with little lipid, and seaweeds need no land or fertiliser, but data are only for two seaweeds and give no information on cost, toxins or vitamins.
steps: Healthy: lipid is low (2.96% and 2.16% of dry mass), protein is 9.56% and 14.89%, and carbohydrate is 23.70% and 25.03%.

Healthy: carotenoids, phenols and flavonoids are antioxidants that protect cells from free radicals; S. linifolium has more carotenoids (3.00 v 2.00) while U. fasciata has more phenols and flavonoids.
Environmentally friendly: seaweeds photosynthesise using sunlight and sea water, so need no farmland, fresh water or fertiliser, and they take up carbon dioxide.
Economic: they grow quickly and can be harvested cheaply, so should cost less than animal protein.

Limits: only two of the three seaweeds are in the table, antioxidant values are in arbitrary units, and there is no data on vitamins, minerals, heavy metals, digestibility or cost; wild harvesting could damage ecosystems.
Conclusion: the statement is supported in part but the evidence is incomplete.

questions.question: Using the photosynthesis equation and the bond energy table, calculate the energy released by photolysis to make one glucose molecule.
steps: In photolysis one O-H bond is broken in each water molecule.
The equation has 6 H2O for each glucose, so 6 O-H bonds are broken.
Energy = 6 x 462 kJ = 2772 kJ.

questions.question: Explain how light energy is converted into chemical energy in the form of ATP.
questions.answer: Light excites chlorophyll electrons; energy from their transport pumps protons, and protons flowing through ATP synthase phosphorylate ADP to ATP.
steps: Light is absorbed by chlorophyll in photosystems, exciting electrons.
The excited electrons pass along electron carriers, releasing energy at each step.
This energy pumps protons into the thylakoid space, creating a proton gradient.
Protons flow back through ATP synthase, and this drives phosphorylation of ADP to ATP (chemiosmosis).

questions.question: State what other information is needed in the bond energy table for the energy of 9164 kJ to be calculated.
questions.answer: The bond energies of C-C, C-H and C-O (single) bonds are needed.
steps: Glucose contains C-C, C-H, C-O and O-H bonds (5 C-C, 7 C-H, 7 C-O and 5 O-H).
The table only gives C=O, O-H and O=O, so only the O-H energy can be used.
Energies for C-C, C-H and C-O must be added so that each bond count can be multiplied to give 9164 kJ.

questions.question: Where in the chloroplast are the bonds of glucose formed? A matrix (printed as a second B on the paper), B matrix, C stroma, D thylakoid membrane.
questions.answer: C stroma.
steps: Glucose is made by the light-independent reactions (Calvin cycle).
These reactions take place in the stroma, not the thylakoid membrane or the matrix (a mitochondrial part).

questions.question: Which row of the table describes how two amino acids join together?
questions.answer: A: carbon and nitrogen, condensation.
steps: Two amino acids join by a peptide bond between the carboxyl carbon of one and the amino nitrogen of the other.
Water is released when the bond forms, so it is a condensation reaction, not hydrolysis.

questions.question: Explain why amino acids cannot be produced from glucose alone.
questions.answer: Glucose contains only carbon, hydrogen and oxygen, but amino acids also need nitrogen (and sulfur), so nitrate ions must be absorbed.
steps: Glucose contains only carbon, hydrogen and oxygen.
Amino acids contain nitrogen, and some contain sulfur.
Plants therefore absorb nitrate ions from the soil to supply the nitrogen.

questions.question: Which row of the table shows where the light-dependent and light-independent reactions take place?
questions.answer: C: thylakoid membranes (light-dependent), stroma (light-independent).
steps: The light-dependent reactions need photosystems and the electron transport chain, which are in the thylakoid membranes.
The Calvin cycle (light-independent) uses enzymes such as rubisco in the stroma.

questions.question: Draw three labelled features on the chloroplast outline, other than the stroma and thylakoid membranes.
questions.answer: Any three correctly drawn and labelled: granum (stack of thylakoid discs), starch grain, DNA (loop), ribosomes, lipid droplet.
steps: Draw a stack of flattened discs inside the oval and label it granum (thylakoids joined by lamellae).
Draw a small oval or round grain in the stroma and label it starch grain.
Draw a small loop or thread and label it chloroplast DNA, or draw small dots and label them 70S ribosomes, or a small droplet labelled lipid droplet.
The label 'membrane' is already given, and stroma and thylakoid membranes are excluded, so these cannot score.

questions.question: Which wavelength of light is absorbed the least by chloroplasts? A 460 nm, B 520 nm, C 600 nm, D 680 nm.
questions.answer: B 520 nm (green light).
steps: Chloroplast pigments absorb blue (around 460 nm) and red (around 680 nm) light strongly.
Green light (around 520 nm) is poorly absorbed and is mostly reflected.
So 520 nm is absorbed the least.

questions.question: State what is meant by the term action spectrum.
questions.answer: A graph showing the rate of photosynthesis at each wavelength of light.
steps: An action spectrum plots the rate of photosynthesis against wavelength.
It shows how effectively each wavelength drives photosynthesis.
This differs from an absorption spectrum, which shows light absorbed by pigments.

questions.question: Which process can be used to separate chloroplast pigments? Options: A (missing from text), B dendrochronology, C osmosis, D PCR.
questions.answer: Chromatography (option A, which is cut off in the text; B, C and D are not pigment separation methods).
steps: Pigments are separated by chromatography, where a solvent carries them over paper or a plate.
Pigments travel at different rates depending on their solubility and attraction to the paper.
Dendrochronology dates tree rings, osmosis moves water, and PCR amplifies DNA, so B to D are wrong.

questions.question: What is the Rf value for chloroplast pigment J on the chromatogram? Options: A 0.625, B 0.800, C 0.830, D 1.714.
steps: Rf = distance moved by the pigment / distance moved by the solvent front, both measured from the origin.
Solvent front: 3.5 + 2.5 + 1.5 = 7.5 cm from the origin.
Pigment J: 3.5 + 2.5 = 6.0 cm from the origin.

questions.question: Compare and contrast the structure of a chloroplast with that of a mitochondrion.
questions.answer: Both have a double membrane, their own DNA and ribosomes; chloroplasts have thylakoids and stroma, mitochondria have cristae and matrix.
steps: Both organelles have a double membrane and their own DNA and ribosomes.
Chloroplasts contain thylakoid membranes stacked as grana, with chlorophyll, and a stroma.
Mitochondria have an inner membrane folded into cristae, enclosing a matrix.
Chloroplasts carry out photosynthesis and mitochondria carry out aerobic respiration.

questions.question: Complete the diagram of cyclic photophosphorylation by writing the correct words on the dotted lines labelled D, E, F, G and H.
questions.answer: D: chlorophyll (photosystem I); E: energy; F and G: ADP and Pi (inorganic phosphate), either order; H: ATP.
steps: D is the pigment/photosystem that absorbs light and loses excited electrons, so it is chlorophyll (photosystem I).
Electrons passing along the carriers release energy, so E is energy.
This energy joins ADP and inorganic phosphate (F and G, either way round).
The product H is ATP, made by phosphorylation.

questions.question: Name one molecule produced in non-cyclic photophosphorylation that is not produced in cyclic photophosphorylation.
questions.answer: Reduced NADP (oxygen is also acceptable).
steps: Non-cyclic photophosphorylation uses photosystem II, which splits water (photolysis).
This releases oxygen and produces reduced NADP.
Cyclic photophosphorylation only produces ATP.

questions.question: Describe the role of photolysis in non-cyclic photophosphorylation.
questions.answer: Photolysis splits water to give electrons to replace those lost by photosystem II, protons for the gradient, and oxygen as a by-product.
steps: Light energy splits water into protons, electrons and oxygen.
The electrons replace those lost from photosystem II, keeping electron flow going.
The protons add to the proton gradient used to make ATP.
Oxygen is released as a by-product.

questions.question: State the meaning of the term biodiversity.
questions.answer: The variety of living organisms, including the number of species, their genetic variation and the ecosystems they live in.
steps: Biodiversity is the variety of life in an area.
It includes species diversity (number and types of species).
It also includes genetic diversity and ecosystem diversity.

questions.question: Explain the role of chlorophyll in the light-dependent reactions of photosynthesis.
questions.answer: Chlorophyll absorbs light energy to excite electrons, which drive the production of ATP and reduced NADP.
steps: Chlorophyll absorbs light energy, mainly in the blue and red regions.
The absorbed energy excites electrons in chlorophyll to a higher energy level.
These electrons pass along an electron transport chain.
The energy released is used to make ATP and reduced NADP.

questions.question: Discuss the effectiveness of the two solvents, propanone and DMSO, in extracting pigments for identifying these seaweed species, using the graphs.
questions.answer: Propanone is generally more effective, extracting more total chlorophyll in all four species, and separates the species better, but DMSO extracts more chlorophyll a in Q and slightly more chlorophyll b in R and S, so neither is best for every pigment.
steps: Total chlorophyll: propanone extracted more than DMSO in every species (P 40 v 7, Q 32 v 25, R 5 v 3, S 16 v 8 ug cm^-3), so it is generally the more effective solvent.
Propanone gives clearly different totals for P, Q, S and R (40, 32, 16, 5), so species can be told apart; DMSO gives similar totals for P, R and S (7, 3, 8), so it distinguishes them poorly.
Exceptions: DMSO gave more chlorophyll a in Q (about 17 v 12) and more chlorophyll b in R (about 2 v 0.4) and S (3 v 2.5), so effectiveness depends on the pigment and the species.
The chlorophyll a : b ratio, used for identification, changes with the solvent (e.g. Q about 0.6 with propanone but about 2.4 with DMSO), so results from different solvents cannot be compared.
Limitations: only chlorophylls a and b are measured, there are no repeats or error bars, and identification would need other pigments, structure or DNA evidence.
Conclusion: propanone is more effective overall, but the method alone is not a reliable way to identify species.

questions.question: Suggest why different concentrations of chlorophyll were obtained using the two solvents.
questions.answer: The solvents differ in polarity and solubility for chlorophyll, so each extracts a different amount of pigment from the same mass of seaweed.
steps: Extraction works by the solvent dissolving pigments out of the cells.
Propanone and DMSO have different polarities and so dissolve chlorophyll to different extents.
The solvent that dissolves more chlorophyll gives a higher measured concentration.

questions.question: Explain why light energy is converted into energy stored in ATP in the light-dependent reactions.
questions.answer: Light excites chlorophyll electrons; their transport releases energy that pumps protons, and protons flowing through ATP synthase phosphorylate ADP.
steps: Light is absorbed by chlorophyll, exciting electrons.
The excited electrons move along electron carriers, releasing energy in steps.
This energy pumps protons across the thylakoid membrane, creating a gradient.
Protons flowing through ATP synthase drive the phosphorylation of ADP (chemiosmosis).

questions.question: Complete the equation for the production and breakdown of ATP by naming the substrates and the type of reaction on the dotted lines.
questions.answer: ADP + inorganic phosphate (Pi) -> ATP (phosphorylation, a condensation reaction); ATP + water -> ADP + Pi (hydrolysis).
steps: ATP is made from ADP and inorganic phosphate (Pi) by phosphorylation.
Making ATP removes water, so it is a condensation reaction.
Breaking ATP back to ADP and Pi adds water, so it is a hydrolysis reaction that releases energy.

questions.question: Explain the role of light energy in the light-dependent reactions.
questions.answer: Light excites electrons in chlorophyll, splits water to supply electrons and protons, and its energy drives ATP and reduced NADP production.
steps: Light is absorbed by chlorophyll in photosystems, exciting electrons.
Light energy splits water (photolysis), giving electrons, protons and oxygen.
Electron transport releases energy that pumps protons, and ATP is made by chemiosmosis.
The electrons reduce NADP, providing reduced NADP for the Calvin cycle.

questions.question: Which row of the table shows the products of the light-dependent reactions that are used in the light-independent reactions?
questions.answer: D: ATP from non-cyclic photophosphorylation and reduced NADP.
steps: The light-independent reactions use ATP and reduced NADP made in the light-dependent reactions.
Reduced NADP is made only in non-cyclic photophosphorylation (cyclic makes ATP only), so oxidised NADP rows are wrong and cyclic with reduced NADP is not possible.
Row D (non-cyclic, reduced) is correct.

questions.question: Simple sugars have the formula CnH2nOn. Name the inorganic molecule from which each of the C, H and O in a simple sugar originated.
questions.answer: C from carbon dioxide; H from water; O from carbon dioxide and water.
steps: Carbon in sugars is fixed from carbon dioxide by RuBisCO.
Hydrogen comes from water, split by photolysis to give reduced NADP.
Oxygen comes from carbon dioxide and from water.

questions.question: Which row of the table shows the inorganic ions needed to synthesise new biological molecules from simple sugars?
questions.answer: Protein: nitrates; RNA: both nitrates and phosphates; triglyceride: neither nitrates nor phosphates.
steps: Proteins contain nitrogen in amino groups, which comes from nitrate ions, and have no phosphate.
RNA has nitrogen in its bases (from nitrate) and phosphate in the sugar-phosphate backbone, so needs both.
Triglycerides contain only carbon, hydrogen and oxygen, so need neither.

questions.question: Draw the action spectrum for this plant on the axes below, using the absorption spectra of the two pigments.
questions.answer: A curve with a blue peak (about 430-460 nm), a low region in the green-yellow (about 500-600 nm), a second smaller peak in the red (about 640-660 nm), and falling to near zero beyond about 680 nm.
steps: Axes are rate of photosynthesis (y) against wavelength 400-700 nm (x).
The action spectrum follows the combined absorption of chlorophyll a and b: a high peak in the blue at about 430-460 nm.
The rate is lowest in the green-yellow region (about 500-600 nm), because little light is absorbed there, but it is above zero.
There is a second peak in the red at about 640-660 nm, lower than the blue peak, then the rate falls steeply towards 700 nm.

questions.question: Calculate how many times greater the percentage of light absorbed by chlorophyll b is than that absorbed by chlorophyll a, at their maximum absorptions.
questions.answer: 1.2 times
steps: Maximum for chlorophyll b = about 85% (at about 458 nm).
Maximum for chlorophyll a = about 69% (at about 430 nm).
85 / 69 = 1.23, so chlorophyll b absorbs about 1.2 times as much.

questions.question: Explain the advantage to a plant of having different types of chlorophyll pigment in its thylakoid membranes.
questions.answer: Different pigments absorb different wavelengths, so a wider range of light is absorbed and more light energy drives photosynthesis.
steps: Chlorophyll a and chlorophyll b absorb different wavelengths of light.
Having both widens the range of wavelengths the plant can use.
More light energy is absorbed, so more ATP and reduced NADP are made.

questions.question: Which row of the table describes the bonds that form between amino acids in a protein?
questions.answer: A: peptide bond between the amino group and the carboxyl group.
steps: Amino acids are joined by peptide bonds, formed by condensation.
The bond forms between the carboxyl group of one amino acid and the amino group of the next, not the R group.
Phosphodiester bonds join nucleotides, so C and D are wrong.

questions.question: Describe how plants synthesise amino acids from the products of the light-independent reactions.
questions.answer: GALP is converted into carbon skeletons such as pyruvate, and nitrogen from nitrate (reduced to ammonia) is added to form amino acids.
steps: GALP from the light-independent reactions is converted into intermediates such as pyruvate.
Nitrate ions from the soil are reduced to ammonium ions, which supply nitrogen.
The nitrogen is added to the carbon skeletons (transamination) to form amino acids.

questions.question: Which row of the table is correct for the light-dependent and light-independent reactions?
questions.answer: B: ADP is phosphorylated, requiring energy, in the light-dependent reactions; ATP is hydrolysed, releasing energy, in the light-independent reactions.
steps: In the light-dependent reactions ADP + Pi is joined to make ATP, which needs energy from light.
In the light-independent reactions ATP is hydrolysed to ADP + Pi, releasing the energy that drives the Calvin cycle.
Only row B has both parts correct.

questions.question: Complete the diagram of part of a chloroplast to show three other labelled structures.
questions.answer: Any three labelled correctly: inner membrane, starch grain, DNA (loop), ribosomes, lipid droplet, lamella (intergranal).
steps: Draw a second line just inside the outer membrane and label it inner membrane.
Draw a small round grain in the stroma and label it starch grain.
Draw a small ring or thread and label it chloroplast DNA, or small dots labelled ribosomes, or a small droplet labelled lipid droplet.
Each label line must touch the structure it names.

questions.question: Compare and contrast the structure of the outer membrane of a chloroplast with that of a thylakoid membrane.
questions.answer: Both are phospholipid bilayers with proteins; the outer envelope is a smooth boundary, whereas the thylakoid is folded into grana and holds photosystems and ATP synthase.
steps: Both membranes are phospholipid bilayers containing proteins.
The outer envelope is a smooth double membrane that controls what enters and leaves the chloroplast.
The thylakoid membrane is folded into grana and contains chlorophyll, photosystems and ATP synthase.
The thylakoid membrane is the site of the light-dependent reactions, which the envelope is not.

questions.question: Where in the chloroplast is RUBISCO active? Options refer to the table labels A P, B Q, C R, D S.
questions.answer: B: Q (the stroma).
steps: RuBisCO fixes carbon dioxide in the Calvin cycle, the light-independent reactions.
Structure Q is the site of the light-independent reactions and is colourless, so it is the stroma.

questions.question: What is stored in structure S? Options: A GALP, B lipid, C starch, D sucrose.
questions.answer: C: starch.
steps: S is the storage granule, 1 to 35 um in size, so it is a starch grain.
GALP and sucrose are not stored in chloroplast granules, and lipid is stored as small droplets.

questions.question: Where is GP (glycerate 3-phosphate) formed? Options refer to the table labels A P, B Q, C R, D S.
questions.answer: B: Q (the stroma).
steps: GP (glycerate 3-phosphate) is the first product when RuBP combines with carbon dioxide, catalysed by RuBisCO.
This happens in the Calvin cycle in the stroma, which is Q.

questions.question: Which is the correct order of size, smallest to largest, for the structures P, R and S? Options: A PRS, B PSR, C RSP, D SRP.
questions.answer: A: P R S.
steps: P is a ribosome of about 20 nm = 0.02 um.
R is a thylakoid space, largest 4.35 x 10^-4 mm = 0.435 um (435 nm).
S is a starch grain of 1 to 35 um.
Smallest to largest: P (0.02 um), R (0.435 um), S (1 to 35 um).

questions.question: Which could be the units for rate of photosynthesis? A mg CO2 produced mm^-2 hr^-1, B mg CO2 produced mm^-1 hr^-2, C mg CO2 used mm^-2 hr^-1, D mg CO2 used mm^-1 hr^-2.
questions.answer: C mg CO2 used mm^-2 hr^-1.
steps: Photosynthesis uses CO2, so the rate is measured as CO2 used, not produced.
Rate is per unit area of leaf (mm^-2) and per unit time (hr^-1).
Option C has both correct features.

questions.question: Compare and contrast the rate of photosynthesis of Spartina and Leucopoa at different temperatures, using the graph.
questions.answer: Both rise to an optimum then fall, but Spartina has a much higher maximum (about 40 a.u. at about 35 C) than Leucopoa (about 16 a.u. at about 20-25 C), and Leucopoa is faster only below about 15 C.
steps: Similarity: both species show an increase in rate to a maximum then a decrease, as enzymes become less effective above the optimum.
Spartina rises steeply from about 10 a.u. at 10 C to about 40 a.u. at 35 C, whereas Leucopoa rises only slightly, from about 13 to about 16.5 a.u.
The optimum is higher for Spartina (about 35 C) than for Leucopoa (about 20-25 C).
Below about 15 C Leucopoa has the higher rate; above that Spartina is higher, and at 40 C it is about 36 a.u. against 9 a.u.

questions.question: Describe how a Q10 value for the rate of photosynthesis can be calculated using the graph.
questions.answer: Q10 = rate at (T + 10) C divided by rate at T C, read from the graph; e.g. Spartina 20 to 30 C: 37 / 21 = 1.8.
steps: Choose two temperatures 10 C apart on the rising part of the curve for one species, e.g. 20 C and 30 C.
Read the rate of photosynthesis at each from the graph (Spartina about 21 a.u. at 20 C and about 37 a.u. at 30 C).
Divide the rate at the higher temperature by the rate at the lower: 37 / 21 = about 1.8.

questions.question: Explain in which of the two North American regions Spartina is most likely to grow, using both graphs.
questions.answer: Wheatland: Spartina needs high temperatures (optimum about 35 C) and Wheatland is warmer, with maximum temperatures of 27-31 C from June to August.
steps: Spartina has its highest rate of photosynthesis (about 40 a.u.) at about 35 C and a low rate (about 10 a.u.) at 10-15 C.
Wheatland has maximum temperatures above 20 C from May to September, reaching about 31 C in July, close to the optimum for Spartina.
Pole Mountain never exceeds about 24 C and is below 15 C for most of the year, where Spartina photosynthesises slowly, so it would grow poorly there.

questions.question: Explain the importance of magnesium ions to a plant.
questions.answer: Magnesium is a central component of chlorophyll, so without it light cannot be absorbed efficiently and photosynthesis is reduced.
steps: Magnesium ions are the central atom of the chlorophyll molecule.
Without magnesium, chlorophyll cannot be made properly.
Less light is absorbed, so less ATP and reduced NADP are produced and photosynthesis falls.

questions.question: Explain why the student concluded that magnesium ions are taken up by active transport, using the graph of uptake in the presence and absence of oxygen.
questions.answer: Uptake is greater with oxygen (270 a.u. at 100 min) and levels off without oxygen (about 120 a.u. from 60 min), so uptake depends on aerobic respiration making ATP, which is active transport.
steps: With oxygen, uptake keeps rising to about 270 a.u. at 100 min, but without oxygen it levels off at about 120 a.u. after about 60 min.
Oxygen is needed for aerobic respiration, which makes most of the cell's ATP, so removing oxygen reduces the ATP supply.
Uptake that depends on ATP from respiration is active transport, which uses ATP to drive carrier proteins.
Some uptake still occurs without oxygen, probably by diffusion and the use of ATP from anaerobic respiration, but it is much lower.

questions.question: Which labelled structure in the photosynthetic bacterium contains the genes coding for the enzymes of photosynthesis? Options: A P, B Q, C R, D T.
questions.answer: C: R (the circular DNA).
steps: Genes are made of DNA; in a bacterium this is a single circular chromosome in the cytoplasm.
R points to the looped DNA, so R contains the genes for the photosynthetic enzymes.

questions.question: Where do the light-dependent reactions take place in the photosynthetic bacterium? Options: A Q, B S, C T, D U.
questions.answer: C: T (the cell surface membrane and its infoldings).
steps: Bacteria have no chloroplasts, so the pigments and electron carriers of the light-dependent reactions are in the cell surface membrane.
T points to this membrane (with its infoldings), which is the site of the light-dependent reactions.

questions.question: Where do the light-independent reactions take place in the photosynthetic bacterium? Options: A Q, B S, C T, D U.
questions.answer: B: S (the cytoplasm).
steps: The light-independent reactions use soluble enzymes such as RuBisCO.
These are in the cytoplasm, which S labels, as there is no chloroplast stroma.

questions.question: Describe two conclusions about the differences in absorption spectra of the plant and the bacterium.
questions.answer: The bacterium absorbs strongly in the near infrared (peaks at about 800 nm and 880 nm) where the plant absorbs almost nothing, and it absorbs very little in the red (about 0.15 a.u. at 650-700 nm) where the plant has a high peak (0.58 a.u. at about 690 nm).
steps: Conclusion 1: the bacterium absorbs wavelengths above 750 nm (peaks about 0.72 at 800 nm and 0.85 at 880 nm), but the plant absorbs almost none above 760 nm.
Conclusion 2: the plant has a large red absorption peak (about 0.58 at 690 nm) but the bacterium has its lowest absorbance there (about 0.15), so it uses different pigments from the plant.
Other points: the plant has two main peaks (blue at about 440 nm, 0.64, and red), the bacterium has several peaks (370 nm, 480 nm, 580 nm, 800 nm, 880 nm) and a wider range of absorption.

questions.question: Describe the measurements taken from a chromatogram and how they are used to calculate the Rf value for a pigment.
questions.answer: Measure the distance from the baseline to the centre of the pigment spot and to the solvent front; Rf = pigment distance / solvent front distance.
steps: Draw a pencil baseline near the bottom of the chromatogram and mark the origin.
Measure the distance from the baseline to the centre of the pigment spot.
Measure the distance from the baseline to the solvent front.
Divide the pigment distance by the solvent front distance; Rf is a value between 0 and 1.

questions.question: Which is the site of photolysis in the chloroplast diagram? Options: A P, B R, C T, D V.
questions.answer: C: T (the thylakoid membrane).
steps: Photolysis (splitting of water) is carried out by photosystem II.
Photosystem II is in the thylakoid membranes, which T labels.

questions.question: Which structure in the chloroplast diagram contains a gene coding for RUBISCO? Options: A P, B Q, C S, D V.
questions.answer: D: V (the chloroplast DNA).
steps: A gene is a length of DNA.
The loop of DNA in the stroma, labelled V, contains genes such as the one for the large subunit of RuBisCO.

questions.question: Where do hydrogen ions accumulate for use in photosynthesis? Options: A Q, B R, C S, D V.
questions.answer: C: S (the thylakoid space).
steps: Protons are pumped into the thylakoid space, which is inside the thylakoid stack.
They accumulate there to form the proton gradient that drives ATP synthase; S points to this thylakoid.

questions.question: How many of the structures labelled P, T, U and W are made of phospholipids? Options: A 1, B 2, C 3, D 4.
steps: Phospholipids make up membranes.
T (thylakoid membrane), U (inner membrane) and W (outer membrane) are membranes, so 3.
P is a ribosome, made of RNA and protein, not phospholipid.

questions.question: Which describes a phospholipid? A glycerol attached to two fatty acids and one phosphate group, B glycerol attached to two fatty acids and two phosphate groups, C glycerol attached to three fatty acids and one phosphate group, D glycerol attached to three fatty acids and two phosphate groups.
questions.answer: A glycerol attached to two fatty acids and one phosphate group.
steps: A phospholipid has a glycerol backbone with two fatty acid tails.
The third glycerol carbon carries one phosphate group, which makes the head polar.
Options B, C and D describe the wrong number of fatty acids or phosphates.

questions.question: The length of a cell was measured and found to be 0.0085 cm. The ratio of the length of this cell to the length of a chloroplast was 11.7 : 1. Calculate the length of this chloroplast. Give your answer in micrometres (um) to 2 significant figures.
steps: Convert the cell length to micrometres: 0.0085 cm = 0.085 mm = 85 um.
The ratio cell : chloroplast is 11.7 : 1, so chloroplast = 85 / 11.7.
85 / 11.7 = 7.265 = 7.3 um to 2 significant figures.

questions.question: Explain the role of the products of the light-dependent reactions in the Calvin cycle.
questions.answer: ATP provides energy to convert GP into GALP, and reduced NADP supplies hydrogen to reduce GP to GALP.
steps: CO2 is fixed onto RuBP by RuBisCO, forming GP.
ATP from the light-dependent reactions phosphorylates GP, giving it energy.
Reduced NADP supplies hydrogen to reduce this compound to GALP.
Some GALP regenerates RuBP so that the cycle continues.

questions.topic: Rate Of Decrease In Carbon Fixation
questions.question: Calculate the rate of decrease of net carbon fixation at 12 00 hours, including units.
questions.answer: About 2 a.u. hour^-1 (a decrease of about 2 arbitrary units per hour; accept about 1.5 to 2.5).
steps: Draw a tangent to the curve at 12 00 hours, where net carbon fixation is about 20.5 a.u. and falling.
Choose two points on the tangent, e.g. about 22.5 a.u. at 11 00 hours and about 18.5 a.u. at 13 00 hours.
So the rate of decrease is about 2 a.u. per hour.

questions.question: Suggest an explanation for the decrease in net carbon fixation between 12 00 and 13 00 hours.
questions.answer: At midday transpiration is high, so stomata partly close to save water, reducing CO2 entry and carbon fixation.
steps: At midday, light and temperature are high, so transpiration is high.
To conserve water, guard cells close the stomata.
Less CO2 enters the leaf, so the Calvin cycle fixes less carbon.
Net carbon fixation therefore falls.

questions.question: Suggest why net carbon fixation was negative before 05 00 hours and after 19 00 hours.
questions.answer: There is no light, so photosynthesis stops, but respiration continues and releases CO2, giving a net loss.
steps: Before dawn and after dusk there is no light for the light-dependent reactions.
Photosynthesis therefore stops or is negligible.
Respiration continues in all living cells and releases carbon dioxide.
The net carbon fixation is negative because more CO2 is released than fixed.

questions.question: Describe how carbon becomes incorporated into plant biomass.
questions.answer: CO2 is fixed by RuBisCO onto RuBP, reduced to GALP and then glucose, which is built into starch, cellulose and other biomass.
steps: CO2 diffuses into the leaf through stomata.
RuBisCO fixes CO2 onto RuBP, forming GP.
GP is reduced to GALP, which is converted to glucose.
Glucose is built into starch, cellulose and other organic molecules that make up biomass.

questions.question: Explain why air temperature affects the CO2 fertilisation effect.
questions.answer: Photosynthesis is enzyme-controlled, so rising temperature speeds it up until the optimum; above it, enzymes such as RuBisCO denature.
steps: The CO2 fertilisation effect depends on how fast photosynthesis runs.
Photosynthesis is catalysed by enzymes, whose rate increases with temperature up to an optimum.
Above the optimum, enzymes denature, so the extra CO2 cannot be used.

questions.question: Suggest why soil temperature affects the CO2 fertilisation effect.
questions.answer: Soil temperature affects root enzyme activity and the uptake of water and mineral ions such as nitrate, which limits growth.
steps: Roots absorb water and mineral ions (e.g. nitrate) from the soil.
Uptake depends on enzyme-controlled and active processes, which slow at low temperatures.
If uptake is limited, the plant cannot use the extra CO2 fully.
At very high soil temperatures, root enzymes may denature.

questions.question: Explain why a lack of water in the leaves would decrease the CO2 fertilisation effect.
questions.answer: Low water makes guard cells lose turgor so stomata close, reducing CO2 entry and so limiting carbon fixation and biomass gain.
steps: Lack of water reduces turgor in guard cells, so the stomata close.
Closed stomata stop CO2 diffusing into the leaf.
With less CO2, RuBisCO fixes less carbon, so photosynthesis is limited.
The extra CO2 cannot increase biomass as much.

questions.question: Explain the results of the investigation into the effect of ECM and AM mycorrhizal fungi on plant biomass at low and high nitrate concentrations, using the graph.
questions.answer: ECM fungi raise biomass at both nitrate levels (+20% and +33%), whereas AM fungi give a loss at low nitrate (-3%) but a gain at high nitrate (+20%); the fungi supply nitrate that the plant needs to make proteins and chlorophyll.
steps: The fungal hyphae increase the surface area for absorbing nitrate ions, which are supplied to the plant; nitrate gives nitrogen for amino acids, proteins (such as enzymes and RuBisCO) and chlorophyll, so photosynthesis and growth increase.
At high nitrate more nitrate is available and both fungi increase biomass (AM +20%, ECM +33%).

At low nitrate AM fungi give a 3% loss, because the plant gives the fungus sugars but gets too little nitrate in return, whereas ECM fungi still give +20%, so ECM fungi are more effective at supplying nitrate.
There is no control without fungi, so the result is only a comparison between the two fungal types.

questions.question: Explain the role of light in the light-dependent reactions of photosynthesis.
questions.answer: Light excites chlorophyll electrons, splits water to replace them and supply protons, and its energy drives ATP and reduced NADP production.
steps: Light is absorbed by chlorophyll in photosystems, exciting electrons.
Light splits water (photolysis), replacing the lost electrons and releasing protons and oxygen.
The excited electrons pass along electron carriers, releasing energy that pumps protons.
The proton gradient drives ATP synthesis, and the electrons reduce NADP.

questions.question: Which would be the most appropriate light to use as a positive control? A green, B mixture of green, blue and red light, C ultraviolet, D sunlight.
questions.answer: D sunlight.
steps: A positive control should give the normal, expected response of photosynthesis.
Sunlight contains all the visible wavelengths that chlorophyll absorbs.
Single-colour green and ultraviolet light do not give the expected full response.

questions.question: Explain the results shown in the graphs for the mean rate of photosynthesis and mean leaf biomass of thale cress under blue, amber and red light.
questions.answer: Red and blue light raise both the rate (3.7 and 3.3 a.u. against 2.55) and leaf biomass (0.123 and 0.125 g against 0.093 g) because chlorophyll absorbs them strongly; amber light is poorly absorbed, so rate (2.3 a.u.) and biomass (0.045 g) are lowest.
steps: Chlorophyll absorbs blue and red wavelengths strongly, so more light energy is used in the light-dependent reactions, giving more ATP and reduced NADP and a higher rate of photosynthesis (red +45%, blue +29% compared with the control).
A higher rate means more glucose is made and used to build biomass, so leaf biomass is higher under red (0.123 g) and blue (0.125 g) than in the control (0.093 g).
Amber light (about 590 nm) is absorbed least by the pigments, so the rate falls slightly (2.3 against 2.55 a.u.).
Biomass in amber light is about half that of the control (0.045 against 0.093 g), because little carbon is fixed while respiration continues to use up sugars.

questions.question: Describe three conclusions from the table of pigment content of the leaves under the different wavelengths.
questions.answer: Chlorophyll a is highest in red light (441) and blue light (412) and lowest in amber light (315); chlorophyll b changes little; anthocyanins are almost unchanged by wavelength.
steps: Chlorophyll a content is higher in blue (412) and red (441) than in control light (382) and lower in amber (315).
Chlorophyll b is the same in blue as in control (148) and lower in red (133) and amber (125), so the chlorophyll a : b ratio is highest in red light (3.32 against 2.58 for control).
Anthocyanin content is very similar under all lights (71 to 79 ug per g), so the wavelength has little effect on it.
Amber light gives the lowest mass of every pigment.

questions.question: Suggest two genes whose transcription could be increased by blue light, giving a reason for each.
questions.answer: Genes for the small subunit of RuBisCO and for light-harvesting chlorophyll a/b binding proteins, which code for proteins needed for photosynthesis.
steps: The gene for the small subunit of RuBisCO codes for an enzyme needed for carbon fixation.
The gene for chlorophyll a/b binding proteins codes for light-harvesting proteins.
More transcription of these genes means more of these proteins are made, so photosynthesis increases.

questions.question: Which row of the table shows where the light-dependent and light-independent reactions take place?
questions.answer: C: thylakoid membranes (T) for the light-dependent reactions and stroma (R) for the light-independent reactions.
steps: The light-dependent reactions need chlorophyll and the electron transport chain, which are in the thylakoid membranes (T).
The light-independent reactions take place in the stroma (R), which holds the RuBisCO and other Calvin cycle enzymes.

questions.question: Where do hydrogen ions (protons) accumulate in the chloroplast diagram? Options: A Q, B R, C S, D W.
questions.answer: C: S (the thylakoid).
steps: Protons are pumped across the thylakoid membrane into the thylakoid space, where they accumulate.
S labels the thylakoid (lamella), not the starch grain (Q), stroma (R) or outer membrane (W).

questions.question: The diagram is 16 000 times larger than an actual chloroplast. Calculate the surface area of the actual chloroplast using surface area = 4 pi r^2, given as a whole number in m^2.
questions.answer: About 104 um^2 for a measured radius of 4.6 cm on the printed diagram (the value depends on the radius measured).
steps: Measure the radius of the chloroplast in the diagram with a ruler; the outer circle is about 9.2 cm across on an A4 page, so r = about 4.6 cm.
Surface area = 4 x pi x r^2 = 4 x pi x 2.875^2 = 103.9 = 104 um^2.

questions.question: Explain the advantages of thylakoids in a chloroplast having a large surface area.
questions.answer: A large surface area holds more photosystems and ATP synthase, so more light is absorbed and more ATP and reduced NADP are made.
steps: Thylakoids are stacked into grana, giving a large membrane surface area.
A large area holds many photosystems and chlorophyll molecules.
More light is absorbed at once, so more electron transport takes place.
More ATP and reduced NADP are made, so the light-dependent reactions are faster.

questions.question: Which describes how ATP is generated in the light-dependent reactions? A hydrolysis of ADP releasing energy, B hydrolysis of ADP requiring energy, C phosphorylation of ADP releasing energy, D phosphorylation of ADP requiring energy.
questions.answer: D phosphorylation of ADP requiring energy.
steps: ATP is made by adding a phosphate group to ADP, which is phosphorylation.
Adding a phosphate needs energy input, supplied by the proton gradient.
Hydrolysis breaks ATP down and releases energy, so A and B describe the wrong reaction.

questions.question: Show how the ratio of ATP used to reduced NADP used (1.5 : 1) for one glucose molecule can be calculated from the diagram.
questions.answer: ATP used = 6 + 3 = 9 and reduced NADP used = 6, so 9 : 6 = 1.5 : 1.
steps: The diagram shows 6 ATP converted to 6 ADP when 6 GP are changed to 6 GALP.
A further 3 ATP are used (3 ATP to 3 ADP) to regenerate 3 RuBP, so the total ATP used is 6 + 3 = 9.
Reduced NADP used is 6 (6 reduced NADP to 6 NADP).
Ratio ATP : reduced NADP = 9 : 6 = 1.5 : 1.

questions.question: Explain why only a small proportion of the GALP produced is used to make glucose.
questions.answer: Most GALP is used to regenerate RuBP so the Calvin cycle can continue, and some is used to make other organic molecules.
steps: The Calvin cycle needs RuBP to keep fixing CO2.
Most GALP molecules are used to regenerate RuBP.
The rest of the GALP is used to make glucose, lipids, amino acids and other molecules.

questions.question: Where in the chloroplast is its DNA located? A intergranal membrane, B matrix, C stroma, D thylakoid space.
questions.answer: C stroma.
steps: Chloroplast DNA is circular and lies free in the stroma.
The stroma also contains the ribosomes that use this DNA.

questions.question: Which other structures in a plant cell contain DNA? A amyloplast and mitochondria, B mitochondria and nucleus, C nucleus and vacuole, D vacuole and amyloplast.
questions.answer: B mitochondria and nucleus.
steps: The nucleus contains the main nuclear DNA.
Mitochondria also contain their own DNA.
Vacuoles do not contain DNA, so options A, C and D are wrong.

questions.question: The DNA contains 150 000 base pairs in 105 regions that code for proteins. Which is the mean number of bases in the template (antisense) strand of one region? A 239, B 476, C 714, D 1429.
steps: 150 000 base pairs / 105 regions = 1428.6 base pairs per region.
Each base pair has one base on the template strand, so the template strand has about 1429 bases.
This matches option D.

questions.question: Suggest two reasons why this DNA contains more than 150 000 base pairs.
questions.answer: It contains non-coding DNA (such as spacers or introns) and regulatory sequences such as promoters, as well as genes for RNA that do not code for protein.
steps: Only the protein-coding regions are counted in the 150 000 base pairs.
Non-coding sequences such as spacers and introns add more base pairs.
Regulatory sequences such as promoters and genes for tRNA and rRNA also add base pairs.

questions.question: Describe the roles of the proteins RNA polymerase, ribosomal protein, RUBISCO and ATP synthetase in the chloroplast.
questions.answer: RNA polymerase transcribes genes into mRNA; ribosomal protein forms part of the ribosome for translation; RUBISCO fixes CO2 onto RuBP; ATP synthase makes ATP by chemiosmosis.
steps: RNA polymerase binds to a gene and synthesises mRNA by transcription.
Ribosomal proteins are part of ribosomes, where translation makes proteins.
RUBISCO catalyses the fixation of carbon dioxide onto RuBP in the Calvin cycle.
ATP synthase uses the proton gradient to phosphorylate ADP to ATP.
